Smt. Anasuya W/O Sharanabasavaraj vs The Deputy Commissioner on 18 April, 2023
Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/140475426/
1

 (By Sri. Prashant V Mogali, Hcgp)
 -2-
 Wp No. 101584 of 2023
 This Writ Petition Is Filed Under Article 226 And
227 Of The Constitution Of India Praying Issue Writ Of
Mandamus Directing The Respondent No.1 To 4 To
Initiate The Acquisition Proceedings And Pass An Award
To Those Excess Lands Which Are Mentioned In
Annexure-B Award Passed U/S 11 Of La Act 1894 By The
Respondent No.2 (Regarding Petitioner Land In Sy
No.35A, 35B, 35C Is Concerned) And Disburse The Same
Compensation Amount To The Petitioner.
 This Petition, Coming On For Preliminary Hearing,
This Day, The Court Made The Following:
 Order

The captioned writ petition is filed by the petitioner feeling aggrieved by the action of respondent-State in utilizing the entire extent of land measuring 11 acre 6 guntas while acquisition proceedings is initiated only to the extent of 9 acre 15 guntas.

2. Petitioner who is the owner of the land in question claims that though preliminary notification indicates that only 9 acre 15 guntas is acquired, however the petitioner's grievance is that the entire extent of land measuring 11 acre 6 guntas is utilized by the respondent- State.
3.
To substantiate his claim, petitioner relies on the award passed by the land acquisition officer which is produced at Annexure-B.
Referring to page 3 of the award, he would take this Court through the table furnished at paragraph 6 of the said award.
At serial No.34 he claims that 1 acre 31 guntas is the disputed portion, which is utilized by the State, but no compensation is awarded.
The petitioner also relies on the reference made in the award wherein the land acquisition officer has recommended to acquire additional land measuring 4 acre 16 guntas which is already utilized.
Out of 4 acre 16 guntas, the petitioner claims that his portion measures 1 acre 31 guntas.

If these all significant details are taken into consideration, then this Court would find that the respondents-State has utilized the private property without acquiring the remaining 1 acre 31 guntas in Survey Nos.35A, 35B, 35C.
4.

In the light of stand taken by the contesting respondents, what clearly emerges that the respondents have utilized the private property owned by the petitioner and the same is utilized for the public purpose.
The action of the respondents in utilizing the private property is not supported by rule of Law and same is without acquiring the petitioner's land by following due process of law.
5. Soon after the fundamental right to property was abolished, the Supreme Court recognized the value of the right to property as a constitutional right in Bhim Singh v. Union of India (1981).

2 absence of this fundamental right to property, it relied on the second Fundamental Right of Property, namely the idea of reasonableness under Article 14, to invalidate certain provisions of the urban land ceiling legislation.

entities.text: Smt. Anasuya W/O Sharanabasavaraj vs The Deputy Commissioner on 18 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Though the right to property is not a fundamental right, it is a valuable constitutional right.
The Supreme Court in the case of B.K.Ravichandra v. Union of India (2020), ordered the Centre to return the land to its owners.
The Supreme Court's decisions and the history of the right to property reveal that, while its primacy as a fundamental right has been questioned, it is nonetheless protected by the rule of law.
This court's expanding jurisprudence also demonstrates that it is a valuable right that guarantees basic liberties and economic liberty.
Article 300-A's wording is crucial, and its resemblance to Articles 21 and 265 cannot be overlooked, they are, after all, a guarantee of supremacy of the rule of law.

In a more recent case of Bajranga v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2021), "right to property is still a constitutional right under article 300A of the Constitution,"
the Supreme Court has ruled in a case where the government took ownership of surplus land even though there was none, the deprivation of a right can only be done in conformity with the legal procedure."

entities.text: Bajranga v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2021)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Courts have also acknowledged the State's interference in the citizen's right to property.

It was held in Ravindran v. The District Collector, Vellore District (2020) that the government has no authority to interfere with a citizen's right to property unless it is done in compliance with the law which was later on reiterated in Jayalakshmi and Ors. v. State of Tamil Nadu (2021).

entities.text: Ravindran v. The District Collector, Vellore District (2020)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Jayalakshmi and Ors. v. State of Tamil Nadu (2021)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Recently, the Madras High Court made a noteworthy statement, saying that under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution, the Right to Property has a tight relationship with the Right to Life.

The Apex Court in Vidya Devi Vs. The State of Himachala Pradesh and others observed that the State cannot dispossess a citizen of his property except in accordance with the procedure established by law.

entities.text: Vidya Devi Vs. The State of Himachala Pradesh and others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The obligation to pay compensation, though not expressly included in Article 300 A, can be inferred in that Article.

To forcibly dispossess a person of his private property, without following due process of law, would be violative of a human right, as also the constitutional right under Article 300A of the Constitution.'
6.
In the light of the principles discussed supra, the petitioner, who has lost 1 acre 31 guntas, has a legal right to claim compensation.
Respondents-State is under bounden duty to compensate the land-loser by initiating acquisition proceedings under the provisions of Land Acquisition Act.
The concerned land acquisition officer has already recommended to initiate acquisition proceedings in respect of 4 acre 16 guntas.
Out of the same, the petitioner owns 1 acre 31 guntas.
Therefore, I am of the view that this is a fit case where mandamus lies.

For the foregoing reasons, I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER i) The writ petition stands allowed.

3 ii) Respondents 1 to 4 are hereby directed to initiate fresh acquisition proceedings in respect remaining 1 acre 31 guntas of Survey Nos.35A, 35B, 35C and pass award in accordance with law.
iii) In view of disposal of the petition, pending interlocutory applications, if any, do not survive for consideration and are disposed of accordingly.
